title: Lydia Shop Fire
subject: Contracts
stem:
Lydia, who sells purple cloth from a small shop building she owns, entered into a contract with Peter, a painter, by the terms of which Peter was to paint the interior of Lydia's shop for $1,000 and was required to do all of the work over the following weekend so as to avoid disruption of Lydia's business. Assume the following facts. Peter commenced work on Saturday morning and had finished half the painting by the time he quit work for the day. That night, without the fault of either party, the shop building was destroyed by fire.

Which of the following is an accurate statement?
call: Which of the following is an accurate statement?

choices.A: Both parties' contractual duties are discharged, and Peter can recover nothing from Lydia.
choices.B: Both parties' contractual duties are discharged, but Peter can recover in quasi-contract from Lydia.
choices.C: Only Peter's contractual duty is discharged, because Lydia's performance (payment of the agreed price) is not impossible.
choices.D: Only Peter's contractual duty is discharged, and Peter can recover his reliance damages from Lydia.

rightExplanation: B is correct. When the fire destroyed the shop building through no fault of either party, the thing essential to Peter's performance ceased to exist. Peter's duty to paint was discharged by impossibility (impracticability), and because Lydia's duty to pay was constructively conditioned on receiving that performance, her payment duty was discharged too — the whole exchange died together. Gold Key: discharge kills the contract, but it does not erase the benefit already conferred — the half-painted interior Lydia received before the fire. Peter recovers the reasonable value of the work already done in restitution (quasi-contract / quantum meruit), off the contract, not on it. Silver Key: read this array as a 2×2 — first lock the row (BOTH duties discharged, because a dead exchange dies on both sides), then lock the column (recovery = restitution for part performance). That two-step march lands on B without touching the traps.

wrongExplanations.A:
Its first half is perfectly true — both duties are discharged — which is exactly what makes it attractive. But "can recover nothing" erases the half-job Peter already delivered. Gold Key: restitution for benefits conferred before discharge survives the discharge itself; the contract dies, the quasi-contract claim does not. A is a half-truth that omits the surviving restitution claim.
*.
wrongExplanations.C:
It runs the discharge test in the wrong direction. The question is never whether Lydia's act of paying money is literally possible (paying money is always possible — if that logic worked, no payment duty could ever be discharged, which the choice's own text exposes). Lydia's payment duty was constructively conditioned on receiving the painted shop; when Peter's performance was discharged, the condition failed and her duty was discharged with it. Both duties die together.
*.
wrongExplanations.D: This is the dominant trap (19%). It imports a breach-style remedy into a no-breach world. Gold Key: when a contract is discharged by impossibility, nobody breached, so expectation and reliance damages are off the table — the only recovery is restitution for the benefit actually conferred. D also misstates the discharge scope: Lydia's duty is discharged too, not just Peter's.

c3.label: CUT (C)
c3.text: C's own text defeats it — it keeps Lydia's duty alive because "payment of the agreed price is not impossible." If the literal possibility of paying money kept payment duties alive, no payment duty could ever be discharged. That internal overreach is visible from the answer text without outside doctrine. Cut C.

c3.label: CLASH (row)
c3.text: The array is a 2×2. A and B say BOTH duties discharged; C and D say only Peter's. With C cut, the row question — does the exchange die on both sides? — is resolved by the taught tiny anchor that payment is exchanged for performance: no performance possible, nothing to pay for. The "both discharged" row wins, wounding D's first half.

c3.label: CLASH (column)
c3.text: A vs B fight on a single axis: does Peter get anything for the half he already painted? The splitting fact is in the stem — "had finished half the painting" before the fire. That fact exists in the stem for exactly one reason.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: Apply Gold Key GK-CONTRACTS-IMPOSS-RESTIT-01: discharge wipes out future duties but not payment for benefits already conferred — recovery in quasi-contract, and restitution (not reliance) is the only surviving measure. This kills A ("recover nothing") and finishes D ("reliance damages"). B is the true and responsive residual.

studentScript: "The call is 'Which is an accurate statement?' — so every clause of my pick must be true. I see a 2×2: A and B say both duties are discharged; C and D say only the painter's. First, C: it keeps Lydia bound because 'paying isn't impossible.' Paying money is never impossible — if that worked, no payment duty could ever be discharged. Cut C. Row decision: Lydia's $1,000 was payment for a painted shop; the shop is ash, so there's nothing to pay for — both duties die. That kills D's first half too, and D's 'reliance damages' was already suspicious: reliance is a breach remedy and nobody breached. Now A vs B: does Peter get anything for the half he finished? The stem measured his progress for a reason. Gold Key: discharge kills the contract, not the quasi-contract — he recovers the value of the half-job in restitution. Not nothing, not reliance. Select B."

recoveryPaths.text: You verified the discharge half and stopped reading critically. Recover by treating every quantified-progress stem fact ("finished half") as a paid-for benefit: discharge kills the contract going forward, but quasi-contract pays for what was already delivered.

You tested impossibility against the wrong party's act. Recover by asking what the payment buys: money duties are discharged not because paying becomes impossible, but because the thing being paid for can no longer be delivered.

You reached for a damages remedy in a no-breach world. Recover by running the breach gate first: no breach → no expectation, no reliance. The only door left open after discharge is restitution for benefit conferred.

A.signal: First half matches the winning row (both discharged), but 'can recover nothing' erases the stem fact that half the painting was already finished — a stem fact that exists for a reason.
A.lawyer: Discharge by impracticability does not bar restitution; Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 377 entitles the discharged performer to restitution for benefits conferred by part performance.

B.signal: Matches both locked cells of the 2×2: both duties discharged, plus off-contract (quasi-contract) recovery for the half already painted.
B.lawyer: Taylor v. Caldwell / Restatement (Second) §§ 261, 263 discharge both duties on no-fault destruction of the subject matter; § 377 preserves restitution (quantum meruit) for the part performance.

C.signal: Self-defeating logic visible in the answer text: if the literal possibility of paying money kept payment duties alive, no payment duty could ever be discharged. The choice tests the wrong side's impossibility.
C.lawyer: The payment duty is discharged via constructive conditions of exchange / failure of consideration, not via impossibility of paying; when the performance owed is discharged, the duty to pay for it is discharged with it.

D.signal: Imports a breach remedy into a no-breach world: discharge by impossibility means nobody breached, so damage measures built on breach (reliance) have nothing to attach to.
D.lawyer: Reliance damages are a breach measure; on discharge by impossibility the general rule is restitution for benefit conferred (Restatement (Second) § 377), not reliance recovery. D also misstates the discharge scope — both duties are discharged.

goldKeys.statement: When no-fault destruction of the subject matter discharges a contract, the discharge wipes out FUTURE duties on both sides — but the performing party still recovers the value of work already done in restitution (quasi-contract), and that restitution is the ONLY surviving recovery; reliance damages need a breach, and nobody breached.
goldKeys.trigger: Fire/destruction mid-performance with 'without the fault of either party' language, plus a stem fact quantifying how much work was already done.
goldKeys.unlocks: The twin traps of 'discharged = recover nothing' (A) and 'discharged but recover reliance damages' (D).
goldKeys.authority: Taylor v. Caldwell, 3 B. & S. 826 (K.B. 1863); Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 261, 263, 377.

goldKeys.statement: Impossibility discharge is never one-sided: the duty to pay is constructively conditioned on receiving the performance, so when the performance duty dies, the payment duty dies with it — the literal possibility of paying money is irrelevant.
goldKeys.trigger: Any answer choice arguing one party remains bound because that party's own act (usually paying money) is still physically possible.
goldKeys.unlocks: The 'only the performer's duty is discharged because paying isn't impossible' misconception (C, and D's first half).
goldKeys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 237, 261, 263 (constructive conditions of exchange; discharge by supervening impracticability).

silverKeys.statement: When all four choices bundle a discharge-scope claim with a recovery claim, read the array as a 2×2 and decide ONE axis at a time: first lock the row (whose duties are discharged), then lock the column (what recovery survives) — never evaluate a choice as a single blob.
silverKeys.trigger: Every answer choice contains 'discharged' plus a different recovery consequence — a matched-pairs 2×2 smell.
silverKeys.unlocks: The two-claims-per-choice trap where a student verifies a choice's true first half and swallows its false second half.

remediation.title: Fire Kills the Deal, Not the Half-Done Work
remediation.signal: Mid-performance destruction of the building/subject matter, expressly without fault of either party, with the stem quantifying completed work.
remediation.studentMove: Lock the row first: the exchange dies on both sides — cut every 'only one party is discharged' choice. Then lock the column: half-done work is a conferred benefit, so cut 'recovers nothing' and cut breach-style damages. Select quasi-contract/restitution.
remediation.tinyRule: Discharge kills future duties on both sides; restitution for work already done survives; reliance needs a breach and there is none.
remediation.trap: Treating discharge like breach (reliance damages) or like annihilation (no recovery at all).
